plants.name: Euphorbia pulcherrima
plants.description: Wild poinsettias grow into leggy shrubs and small trees. Their fiery red bracts look like petals and surround small yellow flower clusters. The bracts are leaves that have changed color. They shine against the glossy green foliage in the cool, dry weeks of early winter.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late autumn through winter (roughly November to February) in its native range
plants.location: Southern Mexico and Central America, including the seasonally dry forests of Guerrero and Chiapas
plants.funFact: Poinsettias bloom in response to long nights. They need about 12 hours or more of uninterrupted darkness each day to develop their bracts. That is why they peak around the winter solstice. The Aztecs called the plant cuetlaxochitl and used it to make a reddish dye.

plants.name: Hippeastrum puniceum
plants.description: Large trumpet-shaped blooms in vivid orange-red open on tall, sturdy stalks above strap-like leaves. The flowers appear in southern-hemisphere early summer. They bring tropical color to gardens and warm, open landscapes.
plants.bloomingSeason: Spring through early summer in the Southern Hemisphere, with blooms often seen into December in warm climates
plants.location: Gardens and naturalized areas in warm parts of Australia, such as Queensland and New South Wales, and in South America
plants.funFact: The plant grows from a large underground bulb. Relatives of this genus are the source of the amaryllis bulbs sold for winter windowsills in the Northern Hemisphere. They are forced to bloom indoors around the holidays.

plants.name: Camellia sasanqua
plants.description: This graceful evergreen shrub opens delicate, lightly fragrant flowers while most other plants are dormant. The petals are silky and the centers are golden with stamens. Blooms drift down in snowy drifts beneath the glossy dark leaves.
plants.bloomingSeason: Autumn to early winter (about October to January)
plants.location: Southern Japan, where it is native, and in gardens across Japan, the southeastern United States, and other mild temperate regions
plants.funFact: A close relative, Camellia sinensis, provides the leaves for all true tea. Sasanqua seeds are pressed to make a culinary and cosmetic oil in Japan and China.
